The verb rig has two very different lives — one honest, one dishonest. They are connected by a shared idea: secretly or cleverly arranging something. Understanding both will give you full command of this word.
Meaning 1: To Dishonestly Fix or Manipulate an Outcome

This is the most common meaning in modern everyday English. When you rig something, you secretly interfere with a process that is supposed to be fair, so that the result is decided in advance — usually in your favor or someone else's favor.

The defining idea is hidden cheating. On the surface, the process looks fair. But behind the scenes, someone has already decided the winner.

Examples:

  • "The election was rigged." — Someone cheated so that a particular candidate would win, even though voters believed their votes counted fairly.
  • "The boxing match was rigged." — The outcome was secretly decided before the fight even began. It was a performance, not a real competition.
  • "They rigged the bidding process." — A company secretly arranged for a particular bidder to win the contract, breaking the rules of fair competition.
  • "The stock market was being rigged by a group of insiders." — A group of people were secretly manipulating stock prices for their own profit.

Common things you can rig:

  • an election / a vote
  • a game / a match / a competition / a race
  • a trial / a jury
  • a market / prices / a bid
  • a quiz / an exam

Important nuance: "Rig" always implies that the cheating is concealed. If everyone openly knew the result was fixed, you would use a different word. The dishonesty and the hiding of that dishonesty are both part of what "rig" means.

When used as an adjective, you'll often see: "a rigged system," "a rigged game," "the whole thing was rigged." These phrases carry a tone of frustration — the feeling that you never had a real chance because the outcome was never truly open.
Meaning 2: To Set Up, Assemble, or Equip Something

This is the older, completely honest meaning of the word, rooted in sailing. To rig something means to put together or set up the necessary equipment so that something can function or work.

In sailing specifically, to rig a ship means to fit it with everything it needs to sail — its masts, sails, ropes, chains, and pulleys. A ship that has been "rigged" is ready to go. The full set of ropes and cables on a sailing vessel is called its rigging (a noun), which you can see is directly born from this verb.

Today, this meaning is used far beyond sailing. In general English — and especially in engineering, construction, theater, and climbing — "rig" means to set up, connect, or assemble equipment so it is ready and operational.

Examples:

  • "The sailors rigged the ship before setting off." — They put up the sails and set up all the ropes and gear.
  • "The workers rigged the crane." — They set up the crane with its cables and pulleys, ready to lift heavy loads.
  • "The climbers rigged their safety ropes before ascending the cliff." — They carefully set up and secured their ropes.
  • "The crew rigged the stage for the concert." — They set up the system of ropes, pulleys, and cables used to move lights and scenery.

Rig up is a very common and useful phrase. It means to quickly put something together — often by improvising, using whatever materials are available — so that it works well enough for the moment. The result is functional but may be rough, temporary, or unconventional.

The spirit of "rig up" is: "I made something that works, even if it's not perfect or professional."

Examples:

  • "They rigged up a shelter using branches and a tarp." — They quickly built a basic shelter from whatever they had around them.
  • "He rigged up an antenna from a coat hanger and some wire." — He improvised an antenna that actually worked.
  • "We rigged up a pulley system to lift the heavy boxes to the top floor." — We quickly assembled a practical lifting system.
  • "She rigged up a makeshift curtain using an old bedsheet and some rope." — She put together a simple curtain from available materials.

The key feeling of "rig up" is practical resourcefulness — getting something working without all the proper tools or materials.

Rig out means to dress someone in a particular outfit, or to fully equip someone with everything they need. It is somewhat informal and a little old-fashioned, but you will still encounter it.

Examples:

  • "She was rigged out in a full Victorian costume." — She was dressed up completely in Victorian clothes.
  • "The soldiers were rigged out with full combat gear." — The soldiers were equipped with everything they needed for battle.
  • "He rigged himself out with hiking boots, a backpack, and a compass." — He equipped himself with everything needed for the hike.
How the Two Core Meanings Connect

At first glance, the dishonest meaning (secretly fixing an outcome) and the honest meaning (assembling equipment) seem completely unrelated. But there is a thread connecting them: both involve secretly or skillfully arranging things behind the scenes so a particular outcome is achieved. In one case, it's ropes and sails arranged so a ship can sail. In the other case, it's circumstances and people arranged so a result is guaranteed. The word traveled from the physical world into the social world, carrying that idea of hidden, deliberate arrangement with it.

  • Rig (honest): To set up or assemble equipment so something is ready to function. → "They rigged the crane."

  • Rig out: To dress or fully equip someone. → "She was rigged out in her best clothes."
